newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean workers erupt in fury at new labour law.
newsitem.headline: Korean workers erupt in fury at new labour law.

text.p: Striking workers shut South Korean carmakers and shipyards on Thursday, crippling key export industries, and hospital and subway staff threatened to join an all-out stoppage in fury at a new labour law.

Half a million workers were called out on an indefinite strike by a militant union body in response to the railroading through parliament of a law that challenges decades of job security by allowing worker layoffs.

Some 150,000 workers responded immediately, halting production lines at Hyundai, Kia and Ssangyong group car plants and shutting two Hyundai shipyards and two others, according to the outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions.
The more moderate Federation of Korean Trade Unions instructed its 1.2 million members to join them on Friday.

The government apologised to the public for ramming through the bill, together with another controversial law strengthening the domestic spy agency, at a dawn session of parliament attended only by ruling New Korean Party deputies.
"I feel truly sorry for failing to settle the issues through dialogue and compromise with the opposition," New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo said.
Opposition parties have physically blocked previous attempts to vote on the bills.
Later, the prime minister's office warned of unspecified "stern countermeasures" against illegal strikes as the prospect of industrial and transport chaos loomed.

Vehicles and ships are South Korea's big export items and have underpinned its rise as an Asian "tiger" economy. Unionists at 14 hospitals, including Seoul National University Hospital, the country's leading medical centre, voted to strike from Friday.
More than 9,000 Seoul subway workers decided on a walkout on Saturday, a half day for most Korean workers.
"We are hoisting the flag of a general strike to punish outrages of the Kim Young-sam government," the moderate union federation said in a statement.
The outlawed union umbrella body was further infuriated because it had expected the law would give it legal status next year. It will now be recognised in 2000.

Thousands of Hyundai workers in the southeast city of Ulsan, the centre of violent labour protests that rocked South Korea in the 1980s, donned red headbands, clenched their fists and chanted "unite and fight" in an emotional rally.
The opposition National Congress for New Politics said it would launch a constitutional challenge to the laws.

"The ruling party's action is tantamount to a coup. It shows that the civilian government is turning into one led by a dictator," a party statement said. Party members would wear black ties to "mourn the death of democracy".
Opposition deputies occupied parliament in a silent sit-down protest and vowed to stay until midnight on Saturday.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions said its initial stoppage would begin at 1.00 p.m. (0400 GMT) on Friday and last until noon (0300) on Saturday.
"Workers have nothing to lose any more," said Namuh Rhee, the head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "I see a series of massive strikes in the first quarter of 1997."

Stocks tumbled on fears of damage to an already shaky economy. The Daewoo Economic Research Institute said if strikes spun out of control economic growth next year could be cut to 5.6 percent against an official 7.0 percent target.
But analysts said the labour law, which allows worker layoffs and flexible work hours, brightened the long-term picture by enabling struggling companies to cut costs.
"The new labour act will have a very positive impact on the economy," said Jardine Fleming Securities analyst Tae Chung.
"Short-term, this will come at the expense of strikes, labour unrest and further deterioration of the economy. But this should be off-set by the long-term recovery."

Opposition parties say the bill giving wider powers to the National Security Planning Agency will be used by president Kim to harrass opponents ahead of presidential polls next December. Kim cannot run for a second term but will anoint a successor.

South Korea's version of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) was stripped of many of its investigative powers by Kim under an election pledge to curb the agency once notorious for torture and kidnapping.
The ruling party insists the agency must be given sharper teeth to combat a renewed threat of subversion from Pyongyang.
